From fixing broken procurement practices to rebuilding our defense industrial base, I’m breaking down the 19 provisions I’ve secured to make https://t.co/ZMumrKKaEw

Misconstruing @LockheedMartin’s CEO and other defense leaders’ comments about sustained demand signals for defense as meaning they “thrive on endless war” is intellectually dishonest.

We are in a state of endless war because generations of civilian leaders have no idea how to actually use our military—and the industrial base that underpins it—to achieve our strategic objectives through time and space.

We build credible deterrence by having a strong industrial base with predictable demand signals for the right technology, at the right price, at the right scale, at the right time. Not one of our leaders across the last three generations has figured out how to do this. But it’s not that hard, and it can be done.

The problem is that you misinterpret the goal.

The goal isn’t endless war, or to use our military every chance we get. It’s to establish and sustain a credible deterrence so that we don’t have to. The true mark of strength is not having to use force, while being absolutely capable of successfully doing so at all times in the eyes of our enemies. Having to use force is a mark of weakness—a failure of deterrence.

But this system is short-circuited when government provides inconsistent direction and demand: cancelling programs it said it needed, rolling deliveries forward—or back—and exposing contractors to the massive risk of indeterminable appropriations cycles year after year.

Say you’re a custom shoemaker. You have a unique design, and a big, credible customer wants to buy 5,000 pairs in year one. They tell you they’ll buy a boatload more in years two through seven. They can’t tell you exactly how many, but you need to be ready—and make the manufacturing capacity investments up front.

You do your due diligence. You talk to the leadership and their bank. Even though they aren’t paying you up front, everything looks as solid as it gets.

Hot dog! You go for it!

You can’t make these shoes in your existing space, so you rent a building, upfit it, buy equipment, hire employees, firm up your supply chain, make commitments, and start deploying large numbers of dollars against the customer’s demand.

Then the customer tells you they only need 1,500 in year one and 300 in year two—but they’re forecasting 10,000 per year in years three and four to make it up to you.

You start freaking out. How are you going to pay your rent, machine payments, and employees? Will you have to lay people off? Can you make good on the commitments you’ve made?

You pull every lever available to barely make it work.

You reach the end of year two, ready for the big production run in year three that you desperately need. Then your customer tells you an event outside their control occurred. The board changed, and so did its priorities. On top of that, the customer’s bank isn’t willing to play ball.

Now you’re up the creek. You’ve lost everything. Your company fails, you’ve let everyone down, and your word is meaningless to everyone who invested with you.

Now get rid of the pretend scenario.

Instead of making shoes, you’re making missiles.

The customer is the government. The event is an election. The board changing means new leadership and new generals. The bank not playing ball is Congress failing to fund the promises the Pentagon signaled to you.

Whether your business has several hundred thousand dollars in revenue or several billion, the principles are the same—and the consequences are just as catastrophic, proportionate to the size of your business.

So the CEO of Lockheed—or any other defense company—calling for consistent demand is not evil or dystopian, nor is it suggesting that war is good or profitable.

It’s just the CEO saying, in a politically acceptable way, that his customer—the government—sucks.

And if the government sucked less, maybe Iran wouldn’t be making fun of our stockpiles on X, and maybe we wouldn’t be stuck in another endless war.

This framing is intellectually dishonest.

The right-to-repair provisions in the FY27 NDAA would establish Government Purpose Rights (GPR) as the default for covered technical data delivered to the Pentagon. That does NOT strip contractors of their rights to privately funded intellectual property. Contractors could still claim more restrictive rights, but they would have to substantiate those claims.

Apparently, even asking defense contractors to let our troops repair the equipment taxpayers already paid for is a bridge too far. Our military shouldn’t need a contractor’s permission to stay combat-ready.

My motive is readiness. Contractors’ motive, among other legitimate interests, is profit. Those interests can absolutely coexist, but right now, the balance is coming at the expense of our military’s readiness. That needs to change.

Rural North Carolina has spent years losing healthcare providers while families drive farther and wait longer for treatment. 

I voted to create the $50 billion Rural Health Transformation Program to start reversing that, and now $17 million is coming to North Carolina for three new mental health clinics, opioid treatment in five counties, and crisis teams expanding into six more.

The promise of America has always been that hard work can build a better life and open more doors for the next generation.

I was glad to join more than 100 Hispanic leaders and community members at @LIBREinitiative’s Capitol Connect in Concord to talk about how we keep that promise alive, from lowering costs and growing small businesses to making homeownership more attainable.

These are the messages that make this job matter.

A veteran whose disability claim was finally decided in his favor. A family who got an $8,500 IRS refund after a year of getting nowhere. A constituent who can get to his cancer appointments. A farmer who left our conversation with new hope.

Government should work for the people it serves. My team and I take that responsibility personally, and we’ll keep fighting to get answers, solve problems, and deliver for the people of #NC10.

I have two daughters, and I wouldn’t send either of them to study in China. 

When a government can invite an American scholar into the country and then turn around and jail him on espionage charges, parents should pay attention.

Xi may want 100,000 American students in China. I’d rather see 100,000 more young Americans learning how to outbuild and outcompete the CCP right here at home.

From food you’d recognize at home to combat rations carried by our troops, @BridgfordFoods makes it in Statesville.

I stopped by their facility to see the operation firsthand and meet some of the people who have kept production running in Iredell County for nearly 30 years. Pretty remarkable range of work happening under one roof.

When bad science becomes federal policy, Americans end up paying for it through higher costs, unnecessary regulations, and decisions that can take years to unwind.

Proud to be an original cosponsor and help put a higher standard into law. https://t.co/LqCp0bGVq2

I’m glad Jacksonville is taking it seriously. We need a lot more of this.

roll_calls.question: On Motion to Recommit — Take Care of America’s Veterans Act (H R 9237)
roll_calls.plain_language: H.R. 9237 (Take Care of America’s Veterans Act) addresses veterans’ benefits, health care, counseling, Department of Veterans Affairs personnel, VA infrastructure, and the Veterans Community Care Program. A motion to recommit is the minority's last formal chance to send a bill back to committee before the passage vote. A Yea supports sending it back; a Nay keeps it on the floor for the passage vote.

post.text:
BIG NEWS on Veterans Day! The House has passed one of the largest Veterans’ benefits packages in decades, and as a Veteran myself, I couldn’t be happier to see it finally moving forward.

The Take Care of America’s Veterans Act brings together more than 60 bills to improve health

I never thought I’d have to introduce a bill to stop people from using a gambling loophole to get around Medicaid’s rules, but here we are.

Congress wrote a work requirement that someone could satisfy by reporting $580 in gambling winnings, even if they lost more than they won. That could mean another six months of coverage without working a single hour.

So I introduced the No Gambling for Medicaid Act to close this loophole before the new rules take effect in January, because a work requirement should require WORK! 
https://t.co/FzXYGrxrsz

roll_calls.question: On Motion to Recommit — Stop Insider Trading Act (H R 7008)
roll_calls.plain_language: The Stop Insider Trading Act would bar members of Congress and their spouses and dependent children from buying stocks and would require public notice before a sale. This vote would have replaced that bill with a broader ban that also forces members, the President, the Vice President, and their spouses and dependent children to sell covered investments they already hold. A Yea would have made that swap; a Nay kept the original bill.

roll_calls.question: On Passage — Stop Insider Trading Act (H R 7008)
roll_calls.plain_language: This bill generally bars members of Congress and their spouses and dependent children from buying stocks, and it requires public notice before they sell. A Yea passes it in the House. A Nay votes against passage.

conflicts.caption: These are overlaps in public records, not evidence of a deal. Lobbying can be for or against a bill, and donors' employers didn't necessarily give money.
conflicts.method: Each itemized donor dollar is counted once, under the industry of the donor's self-reported employer; an industry counts if at least one LD-2 client in it lobbied on any bill this member sponsored or voted on.
